title: Who killed the teenager?
subtitle: Young people are being sold the appearance of adulthood while still needing the freedom to grow into it.
author: ATHENA
credit: Illustrative photograph: Amari Shutters / Unsplash. The person pictured is not a subject of this essay.
body:
ARCHIVE EXCERPT · From ATHENA’s “Who Killed the Teenager?”, 20 September 2026.

Teenagers have not literally disappeared. Nor does research establish that media has destroyed adolescence. But the image identifies a pressure worth investigating: the expectation that young people should present a finished self before they have had time to discover one.

## Growing up faster—or performing adulthood earlier?

A teenager can know how to produce a polished image without having much control over her time, money or movement. She can be fluent in the presentation of adult life while still learning how to negotiate friendship, rejection and boundaries. An adult-looking photograph tells us very little about the support she needs.

This is the contradiction at the centre of the “vanishing teenager”: pressure to look complete, alongside the continuing need to experiment. Adolescence requires room for a style that does not suit you, an opinion you reconsider, a hobby you never become good at. Turning every experiment into an identity statement makes that room harder to defend.

## Give teenagers somewhere to be unfinished

But protecting adolescence also requires adults to offer something beyond instructions to log off. Teenagers need accessible places to gather, affordable creative and sporting activities, trusted adults and privacy that is respected. These are priorities for schools, communities and families—not tasks a mother should be expected to perform alone through constant supervision.

Media organisations have responsibilities here too. We should stop using a few polished young influencers as evidence that an entire generation has become adult. We should make room for teenagers who are funny, uncertain, politically engaged, disabled, ordinary or still deciding what interests them. Their value cannot depend on being beautiful, exceptional or traumatised enough to make a compelling story.

The teenager is not extinct. What is under pressure is the right to develop without continually demonstrating that development to an audience. Media can narrow that space, and businesses can profit from the narrowing. Neither process is inevitable.

The answer is not to demand that young people perform an older generation’s version of innocence. It is to let them grow without requiring them to arrive fully formed.

The Athena Perspective.

title: A place for her story. And the bigger picture.
subtitle: Introducing ATHENA: women and children at the centre of the story.
author: ATHENA
body:
EDITOR’S NOTE

ATHENA is a media initiative centred on women and children. This is a space for news, culture and the questions that deserve more room than a headline can give them.

Our focus reaches across borders and subjects: health, education, justice, the economy, creativity and everyday life. Women’s lives do not fit inside one news category. Neither should their stories.

We want to ask who is affected, whose voice is missing and what a development means beyond the announcement. We also want room for the books, ideas and experiences that help us understand each other.

The Athena Perspective.

title: Reading beyond the headline
subtitle: A note on the space we make for books, essays and difficult questions.
author: ATHENA
body:
EDITOR’S NOTE

Some stories need the pace of a news report. Others need time: to follow an idea, sit with a difficult character, or return to a book with new questions.

ATHENA’s culture section makes space for that slower reading. Literature can help us consider grief, power, girlhood and belonging without pretending that one experience speaks for everyone.

An essay is an invitation to think alongside its writer. Here, that means making a clear distinction between interpretation and evidence, and allowing complexity to remain visible.

The Athena Perspective.
